issues.claim: ASP.NET Core apps use server GC by default.
issues.problem: Neither fetched excerpt supports this. The workstation-server-gc page only says that for hosted apps "the host determines the default GC flavor", and the config page gives the default as workstation. I believe the Web SDK sets ServerGarbageCollection=true, but no linked source shows it.
issues.suggestedFix: Add a source that states the ASP.NET Core default, or soften the claim to "ASP.NET Core apps typically run with server GC (the Web SDK sets it); check the effective setting in runtimeconfig.json".

issues.claim: In .NET 10 server GC runs with DATAS by default; in .NET 8 DATAS had to be enabled explicitly, and since .NET 9 it is on by default for server GC.
issues.problem: I recall this being correct (opt-in in .NET 8, default in .NET 9). However, DATAS is not in either cited page's excerpt, and the question's links do not include the DATAS page. The "memory gap between the modes is smaller" conclusion rests on this.
issues.suggestedFix: Add the DATAS documentation page (learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/datas) to links and linkTitles, and confirm there that it is the default in .NET 9 and later and how it behaves with the 2-CPU limit.

issues.claim: when a container memory limit is set, the GC by default caps the heap at about 75% of that limit
issues.problem: The fetched excerpt of the config page is truncated before the heap hard limit section, so the claim cannot be confirmed from the evidence. From memory it is the greater of 20 MB or 75% of the limit, so "about 75%" is fine for a 512 MB container.
issues.suggestedFix: Confirm the wording on the GCHeapHardLimit section of the config page. Optionally state the precise rule: 75% of the container limit, with a minimum of 20 MB.

issues.claim: a dedicated high-priority GC thread per logical CPU
issues.problem: The docs state THREAD_PRIORITY_HIGHEST for server GC threads on Windows only. The scenario is a Linux-style container, so "high-priority" is over-generalised.
issues.suggestedFix: Write "a dedicated GC thread per logical CPU (high priority on Windows)".

issues.claim: It is rarely disabled, for example to save a little memory and a thread in a very small process.
issues.problem: This is a generalisation, not a documented recommendation. The cited page recommends workstation GC with concurrent GC disabled when running hundreds of instances, which is a more defensible example.
issues.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "It is sometimes disabled when many instances share a machine, which reduces context switching; the docs mention workstation GC with concurrent GC disabled for hundreds of instances." Make the same change in ru.

issues.claim: First make sure that it is really the managed heap that grows. Then think about what comparing two heap snapshots taken some time apart tells you...
issues.problem: The hint spells out the core of the reference answer (confirm managed growth, then diff two snapshots). It gives away the plan instead of nudging toward it.
issues.suggestedFix: Use something like: "Before reaching for heavy tools, how can you cheaply tell which kind of memory is growing? And what can you compare to see not just how much is in memory but what is accumulating?" Do the same in ru.

issues.claim: Take two heap snapshots ... do it on one instance taken out of the load balancer.
issues.problem: The gcdump page warns that collection runs through a buffer owned by the target app that can grow up to 256 MB, and that gcdump can cause OOM in memory-constrained environments. The service here is close to its container limit after hours of growth, which makes this risk real. The page also says large heaps can give incomplete dumps on runtimes before .NET 11, in which case a process dump should be collected. Neither point is mentioned.
issues.suggestedFix: Add: "Be careful near the memory limit: the snapshot needs extra memory in the target process and may trigger the OOM kill itself, so take the first snapshot early. If the gcdump is incomplete, take a full dump with dotnet-dump." Do the same in ru.

issues.claim: The tool must run where the process diagnostic socket is reachable: in the same container or in a sidecar that shares /tmp.
issues.problem: The dotnet-counters excerpt supports this (shared TMPDIR on Linux, same user or root). The dotnet-gcdump excerpt does not show it, though the same IPC mechanism applies. The note that the same user or root is required is missing.
issues.suggestedFix: Optionally add "the same user (or root)" and cite the dotnet-counters page note about a shared TMPDIR.
